Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
An [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: A] is said to be diagonalizable if there exists a diagonal matrix [MATH: D] and an invertible matrix [MATH: P] such that [MATH: A=PDP^{-1}.]

Content:
For example, the matrix [MATH: [3|− 4; 2|− 3]] is diagonalizable because
[MATH: [3|− 4; 2|− 3]]

Content:
In general, we have the following theorem:

Content:
> An [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: A] is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] that consists of eigenvectors of [MATH: A].

Content:
Since eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are linearly independent, we can also conclude the following fact:

Content:
> If an [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: A] has [MATH: n] distinct eigenvalues (that is, [MATH: n] simple roots of the corresponding characteristic equation), then there exists a basis of eigenvectors. Thus, the matrix is diagonalizable.

Content:
Let's show you how to use the diagonalization theorem with an example.

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: \lambda_1={\color{blue}-2},] [MATH: \lambda_2={\color{red}1},] [MATH: \lambda_3=-3] are eigenvalues of a [MATH: 3\times 3] matrix [MATH: A], and that
[MATH: [− 3; 0; − 1]]
are the respective eigenvectors. To find an invertible matrix [MATH: P] and a diagonal matrix [MATH: D] such that [MATH: PDP^{-1} = A,] we do the following: .

Content:
First, we construct the diagonal matrix [MATH: D] by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

Content:
[MATH: [− 2|0|0; 0|1|0; 0|0|− 3]]

Content:
Now, to construct the matrix [MATH: P,] we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns:

Content:
- the [MATH: 1]st column is the eigenvector corresponding to [MATH: \lambda_1={\color{blue}-2},]
- the [MATH: 2]nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to [MATH: \lambda_2={\color{red}1},] and
- the [MATH: 3]rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to [MATH: \lambda_3=-3.]

Content:
Therefore, we get

Content:
[MATH: [− 3|1|1; 0|1|0; − 1|0|2]]

Content:
Note: If the matrix [MATH: A] does not have [MATH: n] distinct eigenvalues, it is not always possible to diagonalize it. However, the algorithm to diagonalize any diagonalizable [MATH: n\!\times\! n] matrix is the same as the [MATH: 3\!\times\! 3] case!
